newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM says government in touch with people.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM says government in touch with people.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard hailed his government's first nine months in office on Wednesday, saying it had kept its pre-election promise to "stay in touch with the great Australian mainstream".

In a U.S.-style state-of-the-nation address, Howard told parliament his conservative coalition had provided "honest, competent and accountable" government and restored the basis of a sound and competitive economy.
And, without naming maverick race row politician Pauline Hanson, Howard pledged that all Australians would be accorded dignity and respect regardless of their race or origins.
"Australia is a united, tolerant and harmonious nation. The goal of my government is to focus on those things which unite Australians and not those which might divide them," he said.
Howard's speech came as Australian homeowners were handed their third interest rate cut since the March 2 election, when a Liberal-National coalition deposed Labor after 13 years' rule.
Announcing Wednesday's cut to 6.0 from 6.5 percent, the Reserve Bank of Australia said low inflationary expectations and a firm currency had allowed it to further ease monetary policy.

Howard told parliament that families and businesses were reaping the benefits of his government's economic management. Families with an A$100,000 ($79,000) mortgage had already saved A$145 in monthly payments and would soon save A$40 more.
He added: "Cash flows are under less pressure, and that means business can now undertake the investment needed for faster growth, higher productivity and more jobs".
But opposition Labor leader Kim Beazley, who replaced the charismatic Paul Keating after Labor's defeat in March, laughingly rejected Howard's claims for his government.
"What an exercise in fatuous triumphalism," Beazley told parliament. "Nobody could have accused us of being excessively modest, I do concede, when we were in government."

"But we never had the hide (cheek) to walk into this parliament with such a mouse-like set of achievements and announce them as though we were climbing every mountain, fording every stream, following every rainbow until we find our dream." Howard, whose government leads Labor by around 15 percent in opinion polls, said the economy inherited from Labor was loaded with large debts, heavy deficits and high unemployment.
His government's strategy focussed on establishing the basis for sustained economic and employment growth while introducing action to reduce unemployment.

He said his government was set to reduce the budget deficit by A$7.2 billion in two years without increasing income, company or wholesale taxes. The 1996/97 budget deficit is currently forecast to be A$5.6 billion.

Howard has been repeatedly criticised for his handling of the race debate sparked by independent MP Hanson, who warned in her maiden parliamentary speech in September that Australia was in danger of being swamped by Asians.

Opposition leader Beazley said Howard had encouraged the race and immigration debate and tried to use it to his own party political advantage, only to find the Hanson genie difficult to put back into the bottle.
"That was a bit of leadership that went lacking," Beazley said.
